views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay in the intensive Washington/Beijing negotiations and hold our current posture — do not escalate and do not quit the table. We should continue closing on enforcement language and finalize a deal at the planned summit, while resisting maximal structural concessions on IP and technology transfer that remain the hard sticking points. Escalation now would be self-defeating given the tariff drag already biting our export economy.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is genuinely high for China: US Section 301 tariffs now cover ~$250B of our goods (timeline: List 3 took effect Sept 24, 2018, and combined coverage reached ~$250B), US exports to that market fell 14.1% YoY in Jan-Feb 2019 and total exports plunged 20.7% in February — the weakest start since 2016, with analysts openly talking of a 'trade recession'. Firm-level targeting is real (ZTE denial order, Huawei DOJ charges and Meng extradition request). This sits at the +0.5 anchor of high threat: major export sectors hit, FX pressure, firm-level targeting. Yet this is not existential: talks are the closest they have ever been to a deal — Trump twice postponed the List 3 hike from 10% to 25%, both sides report progress on text and enforcement, Liu He is in Washington, and a late-April signing summit is contemplated. Precisely because the tariff drag is already real and the deal is near, escalation would be counterproductive while full-concession would forfeit our bargaining position on the unresolved structural/enforcement issues. Hence a mild positive action stance toward negotiation without new commitments, and no rollback until a matching final settlement is on the table.
key_factors: US tariffs on ~$250B of Chinese goods already in force (List 1/2/3)
China Jan-Feb 2019 exports to US -14.1%; Feb total exports -20.7%, 'trade recession' talk
Huawei firm-level targeting and Meng extradition proceeding
Talks at crunch point: List 3 hike postponed twice, progress on enforcement text, late-April summit planned
No final deal signed as of April 3, 2019; enforcement and IP/tech-transfer still contested
